name: Corinthian Purple
lede: Corinthian Purple is a dark purplish red from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color, and nothing in our sources explains why the compilers reached for Corinth.

sections.title: A dictionary name, unexplained
sections.body:
Corinthian Purple is Maerz and Paul's name for a dark purplish red, plate 6, row C, column 5 of their 1930 dictionary, with the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 repeating it under the same hex, #7D435A [1]. Maerz and Paul date the name's first recorded use to 1912, eighteen years before their own dictionary appeared, which they take from an earlier source [1]. None of the 29 books in our concordance mentions this name, so whether the city of Corinth, a dye, or a textile line prompted it is undocumented here [1].

In our color graph the nearest named neighbor is [[dark-mauve|Dark Mauve]], 3.8 units away in Lab space, a shade with less red and more blue [1]. A little further out, at 6.2 units, sits [[dahlia-carmine|Dahlia Carmine]] [1]. The Munsell notation for the swatch is 6.1RP 3.6/5.7, placing it in the red-purple wedge the ISCC-NBS calls "dark purplish red" [1]. It belongs with our [[red|red]] family, and because the ISCC modifier reads "purplish," it also sits near [[purple|purple]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 0.08% of 23,781 paintings, 19 of them, as photographed, with the within-painting lens counting 7 [2]. That is rarer than 72% of our named colors [2]. The earliest match dates to 1600, 330 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name, a floor rather than a first, since a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of a dye or pigment [2].
